A ton of AI announcements from OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. California sued OpenAI over the July incident where its AI agents hacked Hugging Face. Between the growing number of escapes, rogue agent "swarms," and AI-assisted hacks, the public likely only knows a fraction of what’s actually happening.

2. Jensen Huang made his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO, apologizing for his "serious mistakes" and saying he'd be honored to return. A source told CNBC the board is focused on whether his conduct put national security at risk. Trump said he "would not mind" (but still backs Tim Cook for the job).

3. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra now sits ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and behind only Claude Fable 5.2 on Artificial Analysis. Testers were not happy though, with one calling it "the worst model OpenAI has ever released." Probably not what OpenAI was hoping for ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

4. The U.S. is reportedly set to label more than 24 AI firms (including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic) as "national champions," with faster chip export approvals and federal financing to sell American AI abroad. The goal is a one-stop shop where foreign buyers can get U.S. chips, data centers, and models as a bundle, rather than turning to Chinese rivals like Huawei.

5. OpenAI published a study of 1,800+ scientists using ChatGPT, who say AI lets them work about 2x faster at the same quality, and nearly 3x faster when writing research code. OpenAI is also opening the free program to up to 200K researchers, with applications for 50K ChatGPT Plus grants opening Nov. 23.

6. Microsoft released 7 new MAI models at Ignite. MAI Code 2 lands within a few points of Claude Opus 5.5 on coding for a twentieth of the price, and MAI Image 2.7 is now #1 on Artificial Analysis' image editing leaderboard at about a sixth of OpenAI's price.

7. Google declared that "the era of autonomous attacks has arrived," warning that hackers now use AI agents to turn new software patches into working exploits with no human involved. As the cost of intelligence continues to go down, I only expect this to get worse.

8. OpenAI signed deals with 4 outside safety groups (Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire) to test its models from inside the company, with access to source code, training data, and staff researchers.

9. Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, a flagship model it says beats Claude Opus 5.5 on 6 of 16 benchmarks. Artificial Analysis has it well behind Opus overall, though (46 vs. 59).

10. Demis Hassabis' drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs raised $5B, saying its AI-designed cancer and immune disease candidates are nearing human trials. Really exciting step forward towards the goal of curing all diseases with AI.

11. Google started rolling out Gemini's Tasks mode free in 6 countries, letting the assistant phone businesses, book appointments, and shop for you with its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.

12. Perplexity launched Frontier Research, a new team that will openly publish models and papers while working toward AI that can do research on its own.

...daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

note_tweet.text:
Highly recommended read.

Self-improving memory is starting to look like an important component for continual-learning agents. 

So pay close attention to this research direction if you are studying recursive self-improvement.

Just last week, I featured a few papers on the topic, and this week both Meta and Google published on it. 

(find more references towards the end)

Meta lets a model design its own memory habits.

Then they train those habits into the model weights.

The goal is to allow the system to learn the memory design (what to memorize, how to memorize, and what to recall).

This work is actually in the same vein as RIME, which I wrote some notes on last week: https://t.co/wLJy6ntdaJ

Meta first searches for better memory instructions (prompts the model to rewrite itself), then fine-tunes the model (SFT with LoRA) on runs that used the best ones. 

RIME, on the other hand, skips the search and uses RL to train one model to solve tasks and write memories, rewarding notes that help on later tasks. It also trains the model to explore so it collects useful information.

Different ways to address the problem. 

More useful links below:

Google Self-Improving Memory for Continual Learning - https://t.co/ons3yOcSkW

How to Train Memory Writing for Continual Learning - https://t.co/wLJy6ntdaJ

Can LLM Agents Organize Their Own Memory - https://t.co/uibQW9oKmD

Continual-ARC - https://t.co/BPAO8Cb0s3

Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents - https://t.co/qxLyIr0DyN

MemCredit - https://t.co/AlrGHCvZ8O

note_tweet.text:
An illustration of both the power and issues with Astra 6.2 in a way that might be accessible: I asked it to create a game in Blender and Unity where you are the pilot of a Coast Guard cutter who travelled back in time to the War of Independence to stop the British invasion of New York.

It made incredible 3D models and a working game with no errors - its even fun to play! But Astra got obsessed with random ideas that didn't make a lot of sense and built them out without asking along with following my instructions: you could put down false buoys to lure the ship in the wrong direction (like the British would understand a modern buoy?) or you could persuade the British ships to go the wrong direction by talking to them, or that you would spend your time rescuing sailors from other parts of the harbor. It didn't even initially have a shooting mechanism until I pointed it out. This is all kind of minor stuff individually, but it was frustrating to have the AI constantly do its own things without telling me, given its instincts were often off, and then have to redirect it constantly. Other models, including GPT-6 Asta, didn't require the same struggle to control and operate. And these same issues show up in academic research and other more serious use cases.

note_tweet.text:
One of the hardest parts about building any benchmark that measures high-dimensional output is making it granular, while also being aligned with human preferences. This especially holds true for document parsing.

Granularity is helpful because it lets you more precisely encode human preferences. Within document parsing, there are many categories of errors across various document dimensions: chart errors, table errors, form errors, layout errors, and more.

Granularity also enables customization - it lets you better choose the dimensions you care about the most and weigh them more heavily.

You can have a granular benchmark using either deterministic metrics or LLM as a judge; they’re not mutually exclusive:
1️⃣ Deterministic: ParseBench-2 splits parsing into 6 dimensions and 330 test scenarios. Each dimension is weighed by human-defined severity (a wrong digit should cost 10+ pts, extra HTML markup costs 0).
2️⃣ LLM as a judge: You can also define granular metrics where each one is measured by LLM as a judge. Our Document Parsing Protocol (DPP) has a comprehensive taxonomy of 140 rules / 516 written checks, each codified by a judge prompt!

Building a benchmark that is granular but aligned is challenging. There’s no free lunch; neither ParseBench-2 nor DPP are ‘perfect’, but they do make an honest effort in advancing every criteria.

We’re shipping a lot more iterations here. Keep your eyes peeled!

ParseBench-2: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX
Document Parsing Protocol: https://t.co/UQ4PeskH78

article.plain_text:
Sciforium’s latest DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash build reaches 1,129 output tokens per second at P90 on four AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, thanks to our traffic-tuned drafters. And no, we didn’t rewrite vLLM or SGLang from scratch in Rust! Here’s how we did it.
Building on our earlier megakernel work, we trained a traffic-tuned drafter to increase how many drafted tokens the main model accepts given a specific data distribution in the traffic, then extended the drafts from five tokens to seven after resolving stability issues. We combined this with Sciforium and AMD kernel optimizations, including our work to fuse intermediate operations and communication. Better drafts let each verification pass advance the response further, while the kernel work improved execution efficiency, turning the engineering improvements into faster output for the user. Before getting more into details, let me cover what speculative decoding is (for those 1% who still don't know) and then I will cover what a traffic-tuned drafter means in this context.
How speculative decoding works
Ordinary autoregressive generation produces one token at a time, with each token depending on the text before it. Speculative decoding uses a cheaper drafter to propose several upcoming tokens, which the main model checks together in a verification pass. The system keeps the accepted beginning of the proposal, corrects it where necessary, and continues. When several proposed tokens are accepted, one verification pass advances the response by several tokens. The drafter’s usefulness therefore depends on how much of its proposal survives that check.
 

Why acceptance length matters
Draft length is how many tokens we propose. Acceptance length describes how much of that proposal we can keep. Consider a five-token draft: if only the first two tokens are accepted, the rest of the proposal does not advance the response. If the first four are accepted, the verification round gets further. A better drafter makes longer accepted sequences more likely, allowing the system to obtain more useful output from each pass through the main model.
This distinction explains why increasing draft length alone can disappoint. If the main model rejects a proposal near the beginning, proposing more tokens beyond that point adds work without adding accepted output. Improving the drafter changes that tradeoff. Once proposals are accepted further into the sequence, longer drafts give the system more room to benefit from those better predictions. That was the motivation for testing seven-token drafts after improving acceptance with our traffic-tuned drafter.
 

How better acceptance translates into faster responses
For the user, what matters is how quickly the complete system produces output. Longer accepted sequences can reduce the number of verification rounds needed to generate a response, spreading the cost of those rounds across more tokens. But generating and checking longer proposals also takes time. Especially, when we increase the draft length, the verification process also becomes more expensive. So, the speedup depends on gaining enough useful output to outweigh that extra cost. Acceptance length helps explain why a configuration might be faster; measuring output tokens per second establishes whether it actually is. This improvement concerns the generation phase of a response, after output begins.
What we changed
We first trained a traffic-tuned drafter on the customer’s own traffic. We asked our existing customers to let us use their traffic to understand what their data looks like and how we can predict the majority of the expected responses in the speculative drafter instead of the main model. The drafters are tailored to their workload and exclusive to each customer.
With improved acceptance, we increased the proposal length from five tokens to seven. The extra two positions created an opportunity to accept more output in each round. Making that configuration usable required stability fixes for seven-token drafting, and the final benchmark includes those fixes. The decision was ultimately a performance tradeoff: the longer proposal had to produce enough additional accepted output to justify its drafting and verification cost.
We also optimized the operations surrounding the model’s major GPU kernels. Intermediate operations, including mHC and projections, offered opportunities for further fusion. We combined operations into fewer kernels and fused all-reduce communication with computation; all-reduce combines the partial results produced across the GPUs. This work targets the overhead of intermediate processing and data movement. Graph execution already removes the gaps between launches, so the benefit should not be understood as simply filling time when the GPUs would otherwise sit idle.
 
The execution strategy also changes with concurrency. Beyond eight concurrent requests, the existing megakernel approach showed diminishing returns, motivating further work on intermediate operations around the major kernels. We also tested running all-reduce on a separate execution stream to overlap communication with other work. That experiment did not help: the overlapping operations competed for memory bandwidth. Fusing computation and communication and scheduling separate operations simultaneously are different approaches, and the latter did not deliver a benefit in this test. This is why we evaluated the execution changes under their relevant load conditions rather than assuming every optimization would help equally at every concurrency.
Bringing the pieces together
The configuration that reached 1,129 output tokens per second combined DeepSeek’s original model weights, Sciforium and AMD kernel optimizations, the traffic-tuned drafter, and seven-token speculative drafts with the stability fixes in place. The result was measured on four MI355X GPUs using a long-context agentic workload. It represents the performance of that complete configuration; the separate kernel experiments at higher concurrency are not percentages to add onto the headline result.
 
At 1,129 output tokens per second, generating 10,000 tokens takes roughly nine seconds, excluding prompt processing and tool execution. We achieved this rate at P90 on four AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs while retaining DeepSeek’s original main-model weights. The gains came from improving how we serve the model: better draft predictions, more accepted tokens per verification pass, and more efficient GPU execution.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a model serving production traffic on AMD GPUs has exceeded 1,000 output tokens per second. It’s a milestone in our work to turn AMD’s hardware capabilities into production performance, and we’ll keep pushing for faster, more efficient inference.
 
Try Sciforium’s endpoints today here and see how they perform on your own workload. You can also start training your own custom speculative drafter today here, tailored to your traffic and exclusive to you. Bring us the workload your agents actually run, and let’s make it faster.
